subject: Communication
title: Groupthink: When Consensus Becomes Dangerous
description: A short lesson to help you apply Groupthink: When Consensus Becomes Dangerous.

hook.text: NASA engineers knew the Challenger O-rings could fail. Nobody spoke up. Seven astronauts died.

buildup.text: Irving Janis defined groupthink: a group prioritizes harmony and conformity over critical evaluation, leading to flawed decisions.

discovery.text: Symptoms: illusion of invulnerability, collective rationalization, suppression of dissent, and pressure on dissenters.

twist.text: Diverse groups with healthy conflict make better decisions. The most uncomfortable meetings often produce the best.

climax.text: Combating groupthink requires structural safeguards: anonymous feedback, devil's advocates, and leaders who speak last.

punchline.text: When everyone agrees too easily, that's not unity. That's danger.

quiz.question: What was a real-world consequence of groupthink that Janis studied?

details.summary: Groupthink occurs when a group prioritizes harmony and consensus over critical evaluation of ideas. It leads to poor decisions because dissent is suppressed, alternatives are not explored, and the group develops an illusion of invulnerability. The term was coined by Irving Janis in 1972.
details.whyItMatters: Groupthink has caused catastrophic decisions from the Bay of Pigs to the Challenger disaster. Recognizing its symptoms can prevent your team from making similar errors.
takeaways: Groupthink suppresses dissent in favor of false consensus
It creates an illusion of unanimity and invulnerability
Preventing it requires actively encouraging disagreement

faq.question: What are the warning signs of groupthink?
faq.answer: Pressure on dissenters to conform, self-censorship of doubts, an illusion that everyone agrees, stereotyping outsiders who disagree, and failure to examine alternatives. When a group makes decisions too quickly and too unanimously, groupthink is likely operating.

faq.question: How can teams prevent groupthink?
faq.answer: Assign a devil's advocate role. Encourage anonymous feedback. Bring in outside perspectives before final decisions. The leader should speak last to avoid anchoring the group. Create a culture where disagreement is valued as a contribution rather than treated as disloyalty.
